item.title: Even if you're not talking politics at work, it's coming to the office with you
item.description: Most employees aren't discussing the latest political polls during meetings or debating hot-button issues around the coffee maker. But that doesn't mean politics isn't affecting the workplace. A study from Texas A&M University found that the political information employees consume outside of work can influence how they feel and behave on the job. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newfound 'baby' planet smashes record for youngest known world
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed a world that’s less than a million years old as the youngest known planet, using data from NASA-funded archives. Called Elias 2-24 b, the baby planet is still whirling in its natal disk of dust and gas. “Our planet-formation models already struggled to explain the previous record holders for the youngest known […] Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Muon rings enable precise calibration of telescopes at the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
item.description: Research initiated as part of a bachelor's thesis in physics at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB) has culminated in a new analytical description of the muon-based calibration of dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes. The work solves a problem that had remained open for more than 30 years because of the geometric complexity of these optical systems: determining precisely how much Cherenkov light produced by a muon reaches the camera, taking into account the shadows cast by the secondary mirror and the camera itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New towns risk repeating past mistakes unless transport comes first, experts warn
item.description: New towns will fail to deliver thriving, sustainable communities unless high-quality public transportation is included from the outset, according to a new report from the University of Hertfordshire. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineers solve puzzle of Arctic sea ice movement
item.description: Arctic sea ice moves and spreads in ways that wind alone cannot explain. A new UC Riverside-led study finds that collisions between individual pieces of ice provide a surprisingly simple explanation for these movements, potentially offering scientists a better way to predict where sea ice will travel as the Arctic warms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Pretty emotional': Rare video shows humpback whale with stillborn calf
item.description: Researchers say the footage is a rare example of "grieving behaviour", after the whale remained with its calf for several hours. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Without bacteria or chemicals: How methanol and formaldehyde form abiotically in nature
item.description: The biopolymer lignin—one of the most important carbon reservoirs in plants and soils—not only decays through fungi or bacteria but can also be chemically attacked by iron linked to reactive oxygen species, without the involvement of microorganisms. When this happens, lignin is converted into methanol and subsequently into formaldehyde. That is shown by a study conducted at Heidelberg University's Institute of Earth Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Loneliness and local news: How 'news deserts' increase isolation
item.description: As local news organizations continue to disappear across the United States, George Washington University researchers are linking shrinking access to community-based journalism to stronger feelings of isolation and loneliness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Circular Rydberg atoms set three records, staying stable for 11 milliseconds
item.description: Rydberg atoms are considered promising building blocks for quantum computers and their precursors, quantum simulators. Researchers at the 5th Institute of Physics of the University of Stuttgart have achieved record values for the lifetime, size, and storage time of circular Rydberg atoms, a special form of Rydberg atom in which electrons move in a stable circular orbit around the nucleus. The findings were published in Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Fuente: The Guardian.

item.title: Dog-guided cameras uncover weasels across Georgia, including regions unseen for 30 years
item.description: University of Georgia researchers recently located the mammal equivalent of a needle in a haystack: weasels. Weasels are extremely difficult to find, so not much is known about their preferred habitats and overall population health in the Southeast. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do some chimpanzee mothers carry their dead infants for months?
item.description: Chimpanzee and bonobo mothers sometimes continue to carry their infants after they have died, a behavior known as infant corpse carrying (ICC). It is widely documented, and many explanations have been proposed, but few have been quantitatively tested. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: T. rex was warm-blooded and had body temperature close to ours, study finds
item.description: Using fossilised teeth, scientists have finally taken the T. rex’s temperature – and it wasn’t too different from our own. Researchers once thought that dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded creatures. Later findings challenged that, suggesting that older dinosaurs were warm-blooded and could control their body temperature. Most scientists agree that Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded, but pinning down the exact core temperature of an extinct creature is difficult. “We can’t just use a... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Iron Age seeds reveal the origins of Iberian wine
item.description: Spain and Portugal are two of the world's most popular wine-growing countries, with regions such as Rioja and the Douro Valley producing millions of bottles every year. This winemaking tradition dates back thousands of years, but its exact origins remain a mystery. To understand how it all started, scientists led by Carolina Royo of the Instituto de Ciencias de la Vid y del Vino in Spain took a step back into the past and studied ancient grape seeds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sliding droplets point to charging mechanism beyond mobile ions
item.description: Whether on a windowpane at home or during the industrial cleaning of computer chips: droplets sliding over solid surfaces become electrically charged. Yet the physical mechanism behind this charging remains a subject of debate. This charging is usually attributed to the exchange of charged particles (ions) at the interface between the droplet and the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earthshot and the science of positive tipping points: How environmental progress can become unstoppable
item.description: It must be tough being a judge for the world's most prestigious environmental prize: Imagine having to choose between an ingenious machine that removes microplastics from a river in Europe or a company in East Africa that sells clean cookstoves through affordable weekly installments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Majority of Americans are tired all the time - and Gen Z women most of all, CDC study finds
item.description: Adults who experience frequent fatigue are more likely to have symptoms of depression and anxiety Fuente: The Independent - World.
item.dc:creator: Julia Musto

item.title: Dogs show human-like brain activity when they restrain themselves
item.description: When we tell a dog "no" and it resists temptation, what happens in its brain? New research from the Department of Ethology at ELTE and the HUN-REN Research Centre of Natural Sciences suggests that dogs may do more than respond automatically: When they restrain their behavior, their brains show a pattern of activity resembling the human neural signature of self-control. The study is published in the journal Animal Cognition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Aqueduct deposits suggest Plague of Cyprian may have emptied Nîmes around 270 A.D.
item.description: Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have gleaned new insights into ancient water management in the French region around Nîmes by analyzing carbonate deposits within the Roman aqueduct that features the famous Pont du Gard bridge. Among other findings, the aqueduct—built around 50 A.D.—was expanded to include an additional water source after 11 years of operation; this event coincided with a historically documented dry spell. A century after the aqueduct's construction, the water supply to the city was deliberately throttled; it is likely that some of the water was… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La ONU alerta sobre posibles crímenes de guerra tras el hallazgo de cientos de cuerpos bajo los escombros en Gaza
item.description: Más de 630 cadáveres y restos humanos fueron recuperados desde noviembre de 2025, mientras se calcula que más de 8.000 personas continúan sepultadas. El alto comisionado de la ONU, Volker Türk, exigió este 16 de septiembre que investigadores internacionales puedan ingresar al enclave para preservar pruebas e identificar a las víctimas. Israel rechaza las acusaciones y asegura que el organismo ignora las acciones de Hamás. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: France 24

item.title: NASA’s Moon Orbiter Spots New, ‘Once-in-Century’ Moon Crater
item.description: It started as a routine data-quality check. But as Robert Wagner, a scientist with NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), scanned a giant Moon map on his computer screen, an unusually large bright spot circled by a dark halo caught his eye, as it implied that surface material in that area had been shaken up. “I […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bone strength study reveals new clues about human evolution
item.description: Bipedalism, or walking on two legs, is one of the key features that distinguishes humans from other apes. But when and why our ancestors transitioned from a life often spent in trees to a life spent almost exclusively on the ground remains a subject of debate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Incarceration may escalate criminal behavior in South Africa
item.description: Allowing petty offenders in South Africa to remain in the community may reduce their risk of committing serious crimes compared with imprisonment, according to a study published in PLOS One by Farai Nyabadza of the University of Johannesburg, South Africa. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most Americans reject political violence, but support can vary sharply by party
item.description: Republicans and conservatives are more likely than Democrats or liberals to justify political violence in 17 surveyed situations, according to a study published in PLOS One by Garen J. Wintemute of the University of California, Davis, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tyrannosaurus rex teeth reveal a body temperature close to the human average
item.description: When picturing a scaled, toothy Tyrannosaurus rex stomping across North America, building nests and eating other dinosaurs, it's easy to forget that scientists have gleaned everything we know about T. rex from clues left more than 60 million years ago. While the presence of fossils in Alaska suggested that this prehistoric ancestor of birds was already on the evolutionary path from cold-blooded reptile to warm-blooded avian, there wasn't a way to take T. rex's temperature—until now. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep ocean, familiar trash: Plastic waste found alongside possible new species
item.description: It's no secret that plastic and other human trash are a problem for marine life, but our understanding has long focused on the ocean's surface. As described in a study published in PLOS One, a more complete picture is coming into focus, revealing that even some of our planet's greatest depths have become home to our debris. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Conserving just 35% of the nation's waterways could sustain freshwater biodiversity
item.description: By evaluating the health of waterways across the U.S., researchers have identified a network encompassing about one-third of rivers and streams that, if conserved and restored, could sustain the nation's freshwater biodiversity in the face of habitat degradation and climate change. Mark Anderson of The Nature Conservancy, U.S., led the new study, published Sept. 16, 2026, in the journal PLOS One. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI reveals novel nighttime feeding behaviors in right whales
item.description: Right whales forage near the water's surface at night, putting them at greater risk of potentially fatal collisions with boats, Jay Kirkham at Dalhousie University, Canada, and colleagues report Sept. 16, 2026, in the journal PLOS ONE. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: We may soon be able to read long-lost ancient scrolls damaged by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius
item.description: X-ray technology and artificial intelligence—along with the discovery of lead in the ink of fragments from a collection of ancient Roman scrolls—could soon help scientists read long-lost texts buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, according to a study published Sept. 16, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Douglas Seiler, an affiliate of the University of California, Berkeley, U.S.; Jacob Michael LaManna of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S.; David Kreimer of the University of California, Berkeley, U.S.; and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hedgehog coronaviruses may threaten cats more than humans, new study finds
item.description: Washington State University researchers have discovered how a group of coronaviruses circulating in hedgehogs invades host cells, a key to understanding their potential to jump between species and their risk of causing a pandemic in humans. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From 10 to 22 years: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's mission has just been extended
item.description: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope hasn't yet reached its Sun–Earth L2 orbit, and it already has some good news. NASA has announced that the mission has enough fuel to potentially double its mission length. Though initially scheduled for five years of observations, followed by a five-year extended mission, the entire mission could now reach 22 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Toilet pellets may help us flush less and save water
item.description: A pellet that dissolves in the toilet, turning the water blue and masking odor after urinating, could help us all save water, according to a first-of-its-kind study from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prime assembly can correct multiple mutations at once, pointing toward universal gene therapies
item.description: Genomic editing holds great potential yet continues to have limitations. Current methods either rely on untargeted gene delivery or short DNA edits that need to be individualized for each patient. A new paper published today in Nature describes a novel genome engineering method called prime assembly that allows long DNA fragments to be stitched into precise, programmable target positions within living cells. This approach may allow for the development of universal gene therapies that can be used for many patients. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gaming the market: Research provides insights for board game industry
item.description: Anyone who has ever damaged a friendship over a supposedly friendly game of Monopoly knows the allure of board games. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Predominantly online friendships linked to greater support for white nationalism
item.description: From social media to the streets of Washington, D.C., the organized white nationalist movement has become more visible in the United States over the past few decades. But the extent of this extremist movement's appeal to the broader public is less certain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: My son has a potentially fatal genetic disease. What should I do with my $1.3 million estate?
item.description: “He is also the sole beneficiary of my 403(b) accounts.” Fuente: MarketWatch.

item.title: Land use and management intensity affect the suitability of habitats for wildlife in Europe
item.description: Common, wide-ranging vertebrate species, such as foxes, may be finding more suitable habitat in towns and cities than in the wider landscape, while rarer species—which live in smaller areas—appear to favor different habitats, according to new research into species across Europe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ice Age carvers used mammoth tusk patterns to create unique art, study finds
item.description: Intricate designs engraved across the surface of 18,000-year-old female figurines carved from mammoth ivory were inspired by the distinctive growth patterns visible in the tusks, a new study published in the journal npj Heritage Science has revealed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spring-like porous crystals could enable chemically responsive microscale materials
item.description: Crystals are usually imagined as rigid objects with flat faces and straight edges. A research team led by the University of Osaka has recently created a porous crystal that grows into a spring-like helix. The team also found that the crystal can change shape as solvent molecules move in and out of its internal spaces. Their findings are published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some governments may hide a budget surplus to justify a tax hike
item.description: It's annual property tax collection season, and with it may come questions about how those property taxes are used and, if there's a tax increase, why. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Celebrates Restoration of Guam Station Damaged by Typhoon Mawar
item.description: NASA celebrated the full restoration of its Guam Remote Station with a ribbon-cutting on Sept. 10, closing out more than three years of recovery after Super Typhoon Mawar devastated the site in 2023. Engineers from across the agency completed the final and most complex step of the rebuild on July 1, when they returned the […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Korine Powers

item.title: NASA Watches Earth’s Weight, Finds Center of Mass
item.description: Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet’s center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth’s center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements. A team, led […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: albarne1

item.title: La NASA lanzó el telescopio Roman esperando 10 años de vida. La suerte y la precisión le han regalado el doble
item.description: El Telescopio Nancy Grace Roman ha sido uno de los grandes logros actuales de la NASA. Su desarrollo fue un éxito, su lanzamiento transcurrió sin incidentes y se espera que en los próximos años llegue a donde ni siquiera el James Webb y el Hubble han podido llegar, aportando datos de interés en la búsqueda de exoplanetas y materia oscura. Esto ya de por sí era un motivo de celebración. Pero, por si no fuese suficiente, ahora la agencia espacial estadounidense ha anunciado que, por una carambola de suerte y victorias técnicas encadenadas que empezó incluso con un lanzamiento antes de tiempo… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: A 6-nanometer vapor barrier insulates ice during rapid heating
item.description: Put a drop of water into a very hot pan, and it can skitter across the surface on a cushion of vapor. This is known as the Leidenfrost effect. Now, scientists have observed a related phenomenon involving ice and an extremely hot surface—on a length scale of billionths of a meter (nanometers) and within billionths of a second (nanoseconds). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Annie Dillard, Pulitzer prize-winning author of nonfiction and nature essays, dies aged 81
item.description: Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, published when Dillard was 28, skyrocketed her to become one of the most prominent nonfiction writers of her generation Annie Dillard, author of the Pulitzer prize-winning book Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, died aged 81 at her home in South Wellfleet, Massachusetts, on Tuesday. Maggie Nelson, Dillard’s literary editor, confirmed her death to the New York Times . Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Culture.
item.dc:creator: Marina Dunbar

item.title: The science behind greener, healthier lawns
item.description: A healthy, green lawn can be the envy of any neighborhood, but how does someone cultivate a yard like that? Assistant Professor of Ecosystem Science Amber Churchill has been getting her hands dirty and digging into the science behind it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D scans reveal how lichen fungi grip algae across cell walls
item.description: Lichens colonize trees and rocks all over the world. They are symbiotic communities between fungi and photosynthetically active green algae or cyanobacteria, in which both partners benefit from each other: The fungal partner relies on the algae for a supply of carbohydrates and, in return, it protects the algae from UV radiation and other environmental influences. The contact zone where the fungal cells and algal cells touch is crucial for transferring nutrients between the two symbiotic partners. Detailed investigations, particularly a three-dimensional understanding of this area between the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau
item.description: Anak Krakatau erupts ash and volcanic gases in this Sept. 5, 2026, image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8. Eruptions are a regular occurrence at Anak Krakatau, a small volcano between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra. Much of its activity remains relatively mild, but it occasionally puts on more […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Curiosity Postcard Celebrates Rover’s 5,000th Day on Mars
item.description: Description While parked at a sand ridge nicknamed “Chocolatal,” NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover used its black-and-white navigation cameras to capture panoramas at two times of day. The first was taken on Aug. 30, 2026, at 9:56 a.m. local Mars time; the second was taken on Sep. 2, 2026, at 5:39 p.m. local Mars time. Those […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Pufferfish taste receptor more versatile than a human's, detecting both savory L- and sweet D-amino acids
item.description: Our sense of taste is critical for survival, alerting us to substances that provide vital nutrients and those that might poison us. Now, a team led by researchers from the University of Osaka has discovered how one such taste receptor in pufferfish can detect a surprisingly wide range of flavors at once. Their study is published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When equity appeals inspire giving to classrooms, what they signal matters
item.description: Online crowdfunding platforms have enabled teachers in great need of classroom supplies to reach potential donors far beyond their school communities. Yet access to more donors does not automatically eliminate the disparities that shape which projects receive funding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Visits Schools Strengthening Florida’s Skilled Workforce
item.description: NASA recently awarded $10.5 million to seven organizations nationwide through its new State Hubs initiative. Space Florida was selected for Project ORBIT, which aims to expand opportunities for middle and high school students, boost enrollment in key career and technical programs, and create a statewide portal connecting skilled workers with aerospace employers. Elaine Ho, associate […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sandra May

item.title: How some cyclists paradoxically start 'from rest' with a non-zero velocity
item.description: Some track cyclists appear to break the rules of physics, but a new study, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, has created a model explaining the illusion. The results suggest that a quick succession of well-timed moves can help cyclists get a head start without actually breaking the rules of the race or the rules of physics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Astronaut Reid Wiseman to Join NFL Fans in Baltimore
item.description: As part of NASA’s new Inspiration Tour, Reid Wiseman, NASA astronaut and commander of the agency’s Artemis II mission, will highlight America’s strengths in space exploration and aeronautics innovation at the Baltimore Ravens vs. New Orleans Saints game in Baltimore on Sunday, Sept. 20. A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a 27-year Navy veteran and NASA […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Measuring milk's carbon footprint
item.description: Every product or service has a "carbon footprint," a measure of the environmental impact of creating or delivering it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Half-billion-year-old fossils rewrite the origin story of starfish
item.description: Scientists have discovered several 518-million-year-old fossils that reshape understanding of the origins of the animal group containing starfish. The fossils show that these animals ate using tentacles rather than passively using their gills, as previously thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Integrated Medical Model (IMM)
item.description: Planning crewed missions to the Moon and Mars involves preparing for the medical realities of long-duration space travel. Factors like cosmic radiation, microgravity, and distance from Earth create unique health considerations for astronauts. To anticipate these needs ahead of time, NASA developed the Integrated Medical Model (IMM). The IMM is a decision-support tool that uses […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Kim Lowe

item.title: Scientists turn seawater into fresh water without harmful brine
item.description: Scientists have developed a solar-powered desalination system that turns seawater into fresh water while removing nearly all of the leftover salt as a solid instead of producing harmful brine. The self-cleaning technology could also recover valuable minerals such as lithium, potentially turning desalination waste into a useful resource. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Quantitative training overhaul needed in ecology
item.description: Ecologists are collecting more data than ever before, but many still lack confidence in the quantitative skills needed to make sense of it, according to a new paper. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dual findings reveal how to control coherence in plasmonic nanolasers
item.description: Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have uncovered two complementary mechanisms that govern coherence in miniaturized lasers composed of metallic nanoparticle arrays incorporated into an optical gain material, also known as plasmonic lattice lasers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newfound ‘Baby’ Planet Smashes Record for Youngest Known World
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed a world that’s less than a million years old as the youngest known planet, using data from NASA-funded archives. Called Elias 2-24 b, the baby planet is still whirling in its natal disk of dust and gas. “Our planet-formation models already struggled to explain the previous record holders for the youngest known […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Mathematician challenges a 2,000-year-old legend about the Parthenon's optical illusions
item.description: One of Athens' crowning jewels is the Parthenon, a classical temple on the Acropolis that overlooks the Greek capital. According to legend, many historians, textbooks and tour guides say the ancient Greek architects who designed it added subtle curves and other variations to correct optical illusions that would have disturbed the building's clean lines. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5002-5009: Tough Planning To Learn More About Wind-Blown Sediments
item.description: Written by Benjamin Tutolo, Professor, University of Calgary Earth planning date: Friday, Sept. 4, 2026 Curiosity has marked several huge milestones (14 years on Mars; 5,000 sols on Mars; 1 kilometer of elevation gain since landing) over the past several weeks, and the team has duly celebrated these remarkable achievements. These celebrations punctuate the rover’s […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Double dip: Sampling contaminants of emerging concern two ways improves accuracy
item.description: Two are better than one when it comes to sampling methods for tracking the location and timing of toxic chemical contamination in waterways, according to researchers at Penn State. The team tested two typical sampling approaches and found that both are needed to accurately assess the variety and concentration of contaminants of emerging concern—pharmaceuticals, personal care products, livestock manure-borne hormones, veterinary antibiotics and pesticides—in a watershed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New species of egg-eating snake discovered in Ethiopia's Harenna Forest
item.description: A new species of snake that feeds exclusively on birds' eggs has been discovered in the Harenna Forest in Ethiopia, one of the last substantial tracts of natural forest left in the Horn of Africa. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging
item.description: Scientists have discovered that some severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging may be driven not just by damaged DNA, but by the body’s overreaction to that damage. When broken DNA fragments leak into the wrong part of a cell, an immune sensor called cGAS can mistake them for signs of a viral infection, triggering chronic inflammation and even interfering with DNA repair itself. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Bondi attacks prompt creation of new institute for emergency care of children in NSW
item.description: NSW Institute for Paediatric Trauma will help doctors, researchers and specialists prepare for trauma cases Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast A new institute dedicated to improving emergency medical care for severely injured children will be established in New South Wales following recent high-profile trauma events in the state. Based at the Sydney Children’s hospital in Randwick, the NSW Institute for Paediatric Trauma will bring together clinicians, researchers and specialists to deliver advanced training and simulations across the health system. Continue… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ima Caldwell

item.title: Growing up in poverty triples young people's likelihood of becoming NEET
item.description: Young people who grow up experiencing persistent poverty are more than three times as likely to be not in education, employment or training (NEET) at 17 or 23 (3.3 and 3.4 times, respectively), according to new analysis of the UK Millennium Cohort Study by the University of Liverpool and the University of Manchester, commissioned by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Caffeine pollution could disrupt crustacean defenses against predators
item.description: While most people are aware of how plastic, arsenic and various industrial chemicals can pollute bodies of water, the effects of caffeine on freshwater environments remain largely unknown. Nonetheless, traces of caffeine, the stimulant contained in coffee and tea, often pass through wastewater treatment systems, entering rivers and streams. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: These tiny travelers need your garden as a pit stop! Join Joel Sartore, Photographer in his quest to save the monarch butterfly ... Ver más
item.description: These tiny travelers need your garden as a pit stop! Join Joel Sartore, Photographer in his quest to save the monarch butterfly ... Ver más Drop your love letter to monarch butterflies in the comments! Tenemos problemas para reproducir este vídeo. Más información Ver más comentarios Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: A 240-million-year-old fossil just changed the dinosaur timeline
item.description: A newly identified 240-million-year-old animal from Tanzania is forcing scientists to rethink the early dinosaur timeline. Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda belongs to a group previously known only from South America, linking fossil deposits on the two continents. That connection suggests Tanzania’s supposed oldest dinosaur fossils may actually be millions of years younger than previously thought. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Microbes can produce adhesive materials from glucose instead of petroleum
item.description: KAIST researchers have demonstrated the potential of using microorganisms to produce a bio-based alternative to petroleum-derived materials for hot-melt adhesives (HMAs). These heat-activated glues are widely used in packaging, furniture, electronics and automobiles. Using Escherichia coli, the team produced a new polymer from glucose and demonstrated adhesive performance and thermal properties that support its potential use as an HMA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Three questions: Putting nuclear waste into perspective
item.description: For decades, one of the major complaints about nuclear power in the United States has been the argument that, after all this time, we still have not come up with a dependable strategy for sequestering high-level radioactive waste, including spent fuel from plant operation. This issue is of such importance that Haruko Wainwright has put it at the center of her research agenda as an Atlantic Richfield Career Development Professor in Energy Studies at MIT and an associate professor in the departments of Nuclear Science and Engineering and Civil and Environmental Engineering. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heating mica to 200°C reveals friction independent of sliding speed
item.description: Through joint research with the U.S. Geological Survey and the University of Tokyo, NIMS for the first time experimentally demonstrated friction completely independent of sliding velocity—an ideal that had never been realized—by heating mica, a layered oxide also used as a lubricant material, to 200°C (392°F). NIMS also clarified that this is caused by the disappearance of defects within crystals at high temperatures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La NASA ha declarado por primera vez a dos astronautas eméritos y seguro que sus nombres te suenan
item.description: Viajar alrededor de la Luna y ver cómo la Tierra se pone detrás de ella, como el Sol cada tarde bajo nuestro horizonte, parece un buen broche de oro ideal para cualquier carrera profesional. Por eso, tres de los cuatro astronautas que componían la tripulación de Artemis II ya se han retirado de dicha profesión. Solo Christina Koch, la única mujer del equipo, ha decidido continuar su carrera. El miembro canadiense, Jeremy Hansen, dejó la agencia espacial de su país y los otros dos miembros de la NASA, Victor Glover y Reid Wiseman, piloto y comandante de la misión, se han convertido en los… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Beach-burrowing beasties may shovel more sand than any other animal on Earth
item.description: At just an inch (2.5 centimeters) long, the sand hoppers skipping across California's Isla Vista Beach at dawn don't exactly look like a force of nature. But a new study reveals that these shrimp-like creatures might be doing more to shape the landscape in which they live than any other animal on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 16-minute train delay shows how a solar storm disrupted Victorian technology
item.description: A 178-year-old mystery surrounding one of the earliest recorded examples of space weather affecting technology has been solved by an international team led by Lancaster University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Mediterranean is getting warmer and saltier at an ever-faster pace—even thousands of meters below the surface
item.description: Across its basins and thousands of meters down, the Mediterranean Sea is getting warmer and saltier. Now, a new study finds it is also doing so at an increasingly rapid pace. The speedup is largest in the central and eastern Mediterranean and strongest of all in the Adriatic, where it reaches all the way to the sea floor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is pasta a type of noodle? The surprisingly serious debate over two beloved carbs
item.description: Certain taxonomic debates resurface time and again. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find the whole grain “sweet spot” for better heart health
item.description: Eating four to six servings of whole grains a day may deliver meaningful benefits for heart health, according to a large review of 87 clinical trials. Researchers found improvements in body weight, waist size, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, triglycerides, and some markers of inflammation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nearly 50 'ghost galaxies' emerge around three hosts, challenging dwarf galaxy counts
item.description: Dwarf galaxies—with a mass equal to about a billion suns, but often considerably less—are the most abundant in the universe. However, because of their low luminosity, they are very difficult to detect. They have mostly been discovered in the vicinity of the Milky Way, in what is called the Local Group, but also, and in large quantities, at greater distances, where current instrumentation cannot distinguish individual stars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
item.description: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxins
item.description: Exclusive: Plastic surfaces form hotspots with an increase of antibiotic-resistant genes, study finds Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria through the soil, a five-year multinational research project has found. The EU-funded project, which has so far resulted in 22 peer-reviewed studies , found microplastics in the soil of all 227 agricultural fields it tested across 11 European countries. The researchers said this poses a global threat , with healthy soils essential for life on Earth. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.
item.dc:creator: Pippa Neill Environment reporter

item.title: Venus may have swallowed its own moon
item.description: Venus may have once had a moon, but new research suggests the planet’s incredibly slow rotation could have doomed it. Computer simulations showed that instead of gradually drifting away like Earth’s moon, a Venusian moon would likely spiral inward until it crashed into the planet, with larger moons falling even faster. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Australia's ancient rainfall patterns more complex than previously believed
item.description: "Sediment and fossil records are a major pillar of our understanding of how the climate works—but climate scientists have gotten something wrong about Australia's ice age," says Dr. Alex F. Wall, lead author of a new research paper published in Quaternary Science Reviews. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Invisible work' of AI falls disproportionately to middle managers, women
item.description: It's a common refrain that AI is changing how we work, but new research conducted by the Notre Dame-IBM Tech Ethics Lab, housed in the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, shows that AI is creating new forms of work and reconfiguring employees' lived experience of work itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weeping whales: Stillborn humpback whale grieving documented
item.description: Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare research observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists “truly astonished” by discovery that challenges Earth’s origin story
item.description: A new study suggests Earth formed almost entirely from material in the inner Solar System, challenging the idea that water-rich material from beyond Jupiter played a major role. If correct, Earth’s water may have been present much closer to the young Sun than scientists previously thought. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nine in 10 UK gambling websites breach data privacy law, study finds
item.description: Nearly nine in 10 (86%) UK-licensed online gambling websites are operating in breach of the General Data Protection Regulation, according to new research from the Gambling Research, Education and Treatment (GREAT) Center at Swansea University published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En los acantilados de Asturias han encontrado un animal que hasta ahora solo conocíamos de Reino Unido
item.description: En 2009, José Antonio Sánchez Féliz, vecino de Madrid, paseaba por los acantilados de la playa de Vega, en Ribadesella, cuando tropezó con unos huesos oscuros clavados en la roca. No imaginó que acababa de tocar un ictiosaurio de 192 millones de años. Tampoco que su hallazgo tardaría 17 años en confirmar algo que la ciencia europea nunca había visto fuera de Reino Unido. Seis expertos, tres países, un solo animal . El anuncio llegó desde el Museo del Jurásico de Asturias . Investigadores de Argentina, Estados Unidos y España compararon los huesos con cientos de ejemplares británicos y… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Isra Fdez

item.title: Forget robots: Scientists turn cockroaches into cyborg first responders that could save lives
item.description: Innovative researchers have engineered cyborg cockroaches designed for use in disaster rescue missions. These remarkable insects possess the ability to locate victims and deliver crucial medical assistance. Outfitted with cameras and injection systems, they skillfully maneuver through debris. This cutting-edge advancement aims to elevate search and rescue efficiency in tough terrains, with hopes for real-world implementation during future emergencies. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: First-of-its-kind preventive phage therapy provides promising results against Salmonella
item.description: The mammalian gut microbiome teems with a delicate balance of bacteria and the viruses that keep them in check, called bacteriophages, or phages. Each bacterial species usually has its own set of phage partners. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New simulations link unusual particle diffusion to yielding in soft jammed matter
item.description: Soft materials such as colloidal suspensions, emulsions, foams and gels often display complex and unusual behaviors compared with ordinary solids or liquids. From a mechanical point of view, for instance, they can resist deformation like solids, but they can also start to flow like liquids when a sufficiently strong external drive is applied. This transition from solid-like to liquid-like behavior, known as "yielding," is central to the physics of soft amorphous materials and to many industrial and biological processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Born-again' star offers rare chance to watch stellar evolution in real time
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed that one of the fastest-changing stars ever observed has entered a new stage of its evolution, offering a rare opportunity to watch a star's life unfold on human timescales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Speeding glaciers drive half a century of polar ice loss
item.description: The longest satellite record ever assembled shows that Greenland and Antarctica have lost 11.3 trillion metric tons of ice since the 1970s, raising global sea level by more than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches)—and that most of the loss has come from glaciers flowing faster into the ocean, not from melting at the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The local costs of remote sensing: Examining the ethics of laser scanning in tropical forests
item.description: Laser scanning, often referred to as lidar, has rapidly transformed how tropical forest regions are studied, monitored and understood across academic disciplines. The technology enables researchers to peer through dense forest canopies, rapidly providing high-resolution scans of the landscape below. This growing observational power is central to the scientific value of remote sensing technologies but also brings into focus the conditions, interests and power structures under which they are used. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
item.description: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars’s south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it’s a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Faster-flowing glaciers fuel decades of polar ice loss
item.description: The longest satellite data record of ice-sheet change ever assembled has revealed that Greenland and Antarctica have lost a staggering 11 trillion tonnes of ice since the 1970s, driving global sea level up by more than three centimetres. However, the new findings also highlight that the story is not simply one of ice melting at the surface. The glaciers that drain these vast ice sheets are also flowing faster, channelling enormous quantities of ice directly into the ocean. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: SpaceX prepares for first orbital flight of Starship rocket
item.description: SpaceX announced Tuesday that it was planning to send its flagship rocket, Starship, into orbit, a key step in its project to one day reach the moon or Mars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
item.description: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in a creek in San Francisco Bay Area
item.description: Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the San Francisco Bay Area when something that didn't look like the rocks she'd been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Should Beijing use its maritime militia as a backup force in the South China Sea?
item.description: China should strengthen its maritime militia to be an extra force to collect information and maintain a regular presence in the South China Sea, where it is coming into frequent conflict with the Philippines. That was the suggestion Wu Shicun, the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, made on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum, an annual defence gathering in the capital attended by security officials and researchers from nearly 100... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Amber Wang,Albee Zhang

item.title: A world 20 light-years away reveals surprisingly organized, Jupiter-like weather
item.description: Scientists from Trinity College Dublin have developed a way to unravel changing weather patterns on distant worlds. Using this approach, they discovered that the weather on a well-studied brown dwarf, SIMP 0136, previously linked to northern lights-like phenomena, is largely shaped by just two dominant processes: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds violence affects millions across US with links to health, economic hardship
item.description: A new national study reveals the widespread reach of violence across the United States, finding that more than half of U.S. adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half have experienced sexual violence in their lifetimes. The U.S. National Study on Violence Experiences Across the Lifespan (USVEX) also shows stark disparities in who experiences violence and how closely violence is linked to economic hardship, mental health and substance use. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: APODScienceAPODAPOD: 2026 September 16 –…Today’s APODArchiveSubmissionsIndexSearchCalendarRSSEducationAboutDiscuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Hubble + WebbHubble Webb’s View of M64 Explanation: Sometimes where Hubble finds darkness, Webb sees light. An […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Students in Gaza ‘devastated’ after plan for them to study in Belgium fails
item.description: Belgian government unable to agree on evacuation of 13 students to take up scholarships at universities Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities have said they are devastated after Belgium’s government hit deadlock on a plan enabling them to leave the war-torn territory. Ahmed Abujami, a 28-year-old doctor in Gaza, said he was “deeply disappointed” after Belgium’s five-party coalition government last Friday failed to agree on an evacuation plan for 13 students and researchers in the territory. Abujami has a scholarship to do a one-year master’s… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels

item.title: Chinese scientists build world’s smallest CT scanner, weighing just 6kg
item.description: Chinese researchers have developed the world’s smallest CT scanner, a portable device designed to produce images of tiny fossils and archaeological relics. Built by the Shandong province-based Rayim, the Xtomo-Cube is about the size of a desktop speaker and weighs just 6kg (13.2lbs). “The device can be held in one hand and is the world’s smallest and lightest CT system, earning it the nickname ‘palm-sized CT scanner’,” Liu Baodong, a senior engineer at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and general... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Chimpanzees give youngsters the tools to learn tricky techniques
item.description: Two-thirds of a century after Jane Goodall observed "David Greybeard" break off a twig to fashion a fishing rod for termites, researchers following in her footsteps have found that adult chimpanzees in Senegal literally hand youngsters the tools for learning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: James Webb reveals Chariklo’s mysterious rings are changing faster than expected
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed surprising changes in the rings around Chariklo, a small object orbiting between Saturn and Uranus. Over just a few years, its inner ring became more opaque while its outer ring became less opaque. The results suggest that rings around small Solar System bodies may be much more dynamic than scientists previously believed. What is causing the changes remains a mystery. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Transparency and trust are the foundations of every successful research partnership, report suggests
item.description: According to research by the IfM Bonn, strengthening research collaboration between universities and businesses requires regional technology transfer networks in which technology transfer offices at universities and research institutions, as well as chambers of commerce and industry, trade associations, chambers of crafts, business-related networks and financial intermediaries, all play an active role. In this way, networking opportunities could be pooled and examples of good practice highlighted. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultra-processed foods linked to hidden muscle fat that may threaten your knees
item.description: Eating more ultra-processed foods was linked to greater fat buildup inside thigh muscles, according to MRI scans of 615 adults at risk for knee osteoarthritis. Surprisingly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for calorie intake, physical activity, and other factors. Fatty changes in these muscles may weaken support around the knee and potentially increase osteoarthritis risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
